analysis.one_liner: Eliminates federal income tax on all dividends and interest received by individuals.
analysis.headline: A bill to make all dividends and interest tax-free, introduced by one House Republican, drew no cosponsors and died in the Ways and Means Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the tax code so that no individual owes federal income tax on dividends from US corporations or on interest income of any kind, effective for tax years after December 31, 1993. It includes detailed rules for how the exclusion would flow through mutual funds, real estate investment trusts, trusts, and common trust funds. The money the government stops collecting has to be made up by other taxpayers or borrowed. The bill never moved past its referral to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Individuals who receive dividends and interest — above all the households that receive the most of it. Excluding investment income from tax is worth the most to the wealthiest savers, since the value of a tax exclusion rises with income and with the amount invested. The bill also writes detailed favorable rules for mutual funds and real estate investment trusts, whose distributions would be reclassified to qualify for the tax-free treatment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy households with large investment income

how_it_helps.text: Removes all federal income tax on dividends from domestic corporations and on interest received by individuals, for tax years after December 31, 1993.

Extends the exclusion through investment vehicles: distributions from regulated investment companies and real estate investment trusts count toward the tax-free exclusion under detailed reclassification rules, and trust beneficiaries are treated as having received their allocable share of tax-free dividends and interest.
Carves out nonresident aliens, who get the exclusion only on US-business-connected income, limiting the benefit to a narrower set of cases.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury and, in the end, everyone who pays taxes or is affected by federal borrowing. Income the government stops taxing on dividends and interest must be replaced by higher taxes on other income, by spending cuts, or by more debt.
analysis.who_pays_short: Other taxpayers and the federal Treasury

drawbacks.text: Excluding all dividends and interest from income tax removes a broad slice of the tax base; the lost revenue must be recovered from other taxpayers or added to the deficit, a cost the bill does not address anywhere in its text.
The benefit is largest for the highest-income households, because the amount of tax saved scales directly with how much dividend and interest income a person has.
The bill attracted no cosponsors, which signaled no committee or floor support even among members inclined toward tax cuts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For savers the exclusion is real money, and a small saver would notice it. But the design is lopsided: because the benefit scales with the amount of investment income, most of the value flows to the households with the largest portfolios, while the revenue loss is spread across everyone else through deficits or higher taxes elsewhere. There is no offsetting provision in the bill to pay for the cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and stayed there; the committee took no action, and it died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. Philip Crane introduced the bill on June 22, 1993 and gave introductory remarks on it the same day.
It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which controls tax legislation, and the committee never reported it out; no hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained directly, since nothing changed. The outcome left in place the existing tax treatment of dividends and interest, sparing the Treasury the revenue loss the bill would have caused. Investors who hoped to keep more of their investment income are the ones who came out short.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo — Treasury kept its revenue

for.name: Rep. Philip Crane
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on it, but recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; sole gatekeeper for House tax bills
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on the day of introduction and never took it up, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no cosponsors joined, so the record shows only a single Republican sponsor and no measurable partisan or cross-party support.

industries.note: They would stop paying tax on all dividends and interest, the largest dollar benefit going to the largest portfolios. The cost shows up as federal deficits or higher taxes on other income paid by ordinary taxpayers.

industries.industry: Mutual funds and real estate investment trusts
industries.note: The bill contains detailed rules so that mutual fund and REIT distributions are reclassified as tax-free dividends or interest, making these products more attractive to taxable investors and routing a new tax benefit through the fund industry.
Tax-free interest makes deposits, bonds, and other interest-bearing instruments more attractive to hold, raising demand for the debt and deposits these institutions issue.
Excluding a broad category of income shrinks federal revenue that must be replaced by borrowing or by taxing other income.
